preoperative survey using MDCT, a single medical

Abstract
This study evaluated multi-detector computed tomography (MDCT) scans per-
formed on potential living donors for adult-to-adult liver transplantation (LDLT), with the
aim of identifying signiﬁcant ﬁndings that could be used to exclude potential transplantation
donors. We retrospectively reviewed the medical records of 151 consecutive potential adult
donors for LDLT from May 2007 to January 2015. Liver parenchyma steatosis, focal hepatic
mass or intraabdominal malignancy, vascular variations, and donor liver volume were evalu-
ated via MDCT. Grounds for excluding potential donors were also recorded and analyzed. Of
the 151 potential donors, nine (6.0%) had moderate to severe fatty liver, 37 (24.5%) had hepat-
ic arterial variants, 22 (14.6%) had signiﬁcant portal venous variants, and more than half were
found to have right accessory inferior hepatic vein. No intraabdominal malignancies were
found. Eighty-eight potential donors were rejected, with the most common cause being insuf-
ﬁcient recipient volume or remnant donor volume (47.7%), moderate to severe parenchymal
steatosis (10.2%), and recipient expiration prior to transplantation (8.0%). An additional 16 po-
tential donors were excluded by the surgical team due to the complexity of their portal venous
variations. The rate of exclusion by pre-transplant imaging evaluation with MDCT was 33.8%.
MDCT can provide accurate quantiﬁcation of donor liver volume and steatosis severity along

Introduction
Living donor liver transplantation (LDLT) is a potentially
curative surgical management for liver failure and liver
cancer with growing global interest [1,2]. It can be clas-
siﬁed into three different types based on the surgical
plane chosen during graft harvest: right hepatectomy
(RH), left hepatectomy (LH), and left lateral segmentec-
tomy (LLS). RH is usually performed in adult liver trans-
plantation, while LH or LLS is primarily reserved for the
pediatric population.
Preoperative evaluation to minimize morbidity for both

donor and recipient remains the highest priority in LDLT [3].
Multi-detector
computed
tomography
(MDCT)
provides
detailed information on potential donors, including (1)
degree of liver parenchyma steatosis, (2) presence of focal
liver mass or intraabdominal malignancy, (3) anatomically
signiﬁcant variations in the hepatic arterial, venous or
portal venous systems, and (4) accurate measurement of
liver donor volume (DV) and remnant volume (RV).
Several studies have described the use of preoperative
MDCT examination for LDLT [4,5], with some authors dis-
cussing important anatomic features [6,7] and volume
measurements [8]. However, studies that correlate these
characteristics with donor exclusion from LDLT remain rare.
Tsang et al. [9] brieﬂy explored potential criteria for
excluding potential living donors in Taiwan with the use of
various imaging modalities, but precise details on relative
and absolute contraindications based on preoperative
MDCT are still lacking.
The purpose of this study was to determine the most
common and clinically relevant exclusion criteria of po-
tential living donors for LDLT in Taiwan, with a particular
focus on factors that can be identiﬁed on preoperative
MDCT survey.
Methods
Subjects
A total of 151 consecutive potential adult-to-adult living
donors were evaluated retrospectively by MDCT between
May 2007 and January 2015. To be included in the study, a
potential donor had to be an adult between 18 and 70 years
of age and a blood relative of the recipient.
MDCT technique and image reconstruction
MDCT scan was performed using a 64-detector row CT
(Brilliance 64; Philips, Healthcare) with multi-phase image
acquisition. Initial non-contrast scanning for hepatic stea-
tosis survey was followed by intravenous bolus administra-
tion
of
100e150
mL
of
non-ionic
contrast
material
(Omnipaque, GE Healthcare, USA) at a rate of 3 mL/s, both
under
the
following
imaging
parameters:
120
kVp,
100e300 mAs and a rotation time of 0.75 s. A real-time
bolus tracking system ensured timing accuracy of the
arterial phase (collimation: 64 �0.625 mm; pitch: 0.92;
reconstruction interval: 1.4/0.8 mm). Arterial scanning was
automatically triggered at a detection threshold of 100
Hounsﬁeld units (HU) in the lower thoracic aorta. Portal
venous phase imaging was started 60 s after the start of
contrast material injection.
Raw CT data were sent from the scanner to a commer-
cially available workstation. Multi-planar maximum in-
tensity
projection
and
three-dimensional
volume
renderings were created for both arterial and venous phase
acquisitions. An integrated liver calculation software pro-
gram (Extended Brilliance Workspace; Philips Healthcare,
the Netherlands) was used for post-processing. The hepatic
venous phase data were used to calculate the hepatic
volume of living donors through software recognition of the
dissection plane. Initially, we outlined the entire liver while
excluding the larger ﬁssures, the ligamentum teres hepatis,
as well as large vessels, such as the extrahepatic portal vein
in the area of the porta hepatis and the inferior vena cava
(IVC). The total volume (TV) was calculated from this se-
lection. Measurements were next taken based on a dissec-
tion plane, which we manually marked according to the
individual harvest planes needed to facilitate the division
of donor liver and remnant liver. Based on these parame-
ters, the software then calculated measurements for TV,
DV, and RV [10](Fig. 1).
Image interpretation
A senior radiologist with more than 20 years of experience
in abdominal imaging and liver transplantation reviewed all
CT images and the following variables were collected.
Liver parenchyma steatosis
Determination of liver parenchyma steatosis was made with
non-contrast CT images. Parenchyma attenuation was
measured in three axial sections of the liver: upper, middle,
and lower portions. On each section, four region of interest
(ROI) measurements were obtained, one in each of the
medial and lateral portions of the left and right lobes,
respectively, with each ROI measuring about 100 mm2 in
size. The average value of these 12 ROIs was then used to
estimate the percentage of macrovesicular steatosis [11].
Mild fatty liver was deﬁned as <30% steatosis, moderate

fatty liver from 30% to 60%, and steatosis of more than 60%
was deemed severe [12,13]. Only the more common mac-
rovesicular form of fatty liver was considered, since
microvesicular steatosis was previously shown not to affect
outcomes in LDLT [14].
Presence of hepatic lesion or intraabdominal malignancy
All images from the multi-phase MDCT scan were carefully
reviewed in order to detect hepatic lesions and rule out
intraabdominal malignancy.
Hepatic arterial variants
To assess hepatic arterial anatomy between the right,
middle, and left hepatic arteries, we modiﬁed Michel’s
original
classiﬁcation
of
hepatic
vasculature
[15]
by
appending two extra variants. Type XI describes a commu-
nicating branch between the proximal left hepatic artery
(LHA) and the right hepatic artery (RHA) in an otherwise
normal hepatic artery anatomy, while Type XII denotes a
common trunk for the origin of the celiac axis and superior
mesenteric artery (SMA). Variations in the origin of the
feeding artery to the medial segment of the left hepatic
lobe (segment IV) were recorded, as well as the presence of
celiac trunk stenosis (Table 3).
Portal venous variants
Intrahepatic portal venous variants were divided into ﬁve
types based on the Akgul classiﬁcation (Table 3) [16] for
portal venous anatomy evaluation.
Hepatic venous variants
Important characteristics and variations of the hepatic
venous system were collected, including (a) diameter of
the accessory inferior RHV and the distance between it and
the conﬂuence of hepatic veins, (b) whether there is a
common stump for the LHV and MHV, and (c) the presence
of venous drainage from segment I into the IVC (Table 3).
Use of predicted TV, DV, and RV
A virtual surgical plane was placed at the avascular plane
that extends along the MHV, for harvesting of the left or
right hepatic lobe. In some cases, the surgical plane was
modiﬁed after consultation with the transplant surgeon in
order to accommodate anatomically signiﬁcant hepatic
venous variants.
The previously calculated predicted DV and RV were
used to select suitable living donors. Predicted DV was
converted to graft weight with a factor of 1.00 g/ml as liver
physical density [17], which was matched to recipient body
weight by the transplant surgeon. A potential donor was
only considered if the graft-to-recipient body weight ratio
(GRBWR) was at least 0.7%, and also if RV in the donor was
at least 30% of the TV.
Statistical analysis
All statistical analyses were performed using SPSS version
22.0 software (SPSS Inc., Chicago, IL). Numeric results were
presented with mean �standard deviation (SD).
Results
The 151 potential donors had a mean age of 35 �11 years
(range: 18e69 years), and included 90 males and 61 fe-
males. Their baseline characteristics and preoperative TV,
DV, and RV results are summarized in Tables 1 and 2.
Liver parenchyma steatosis, focal liver masses, and
intraabdominal malignancy
Moderate to severe fatty liver was found in nine cases.
Peripheral A-P shunting was found in two donors while focal
nodular hyperplasia was found in a single donor. Focal he-
patic hemangiomas were detected in eight potential do-
nors. These had no bearing on the preoperative evaluation,
since presence of benign tumors was not a contraindication
for LDLT at our center. No malignant intraabdominal lesions
were found during preoperative survey.

Hepatic arterial, portal venous, and hepatic venous
variants
According to our classiﬁcation of hepatic vasculature, 114
potential living donors (75.4%) had conventional arterial
anatomy (type I) and 37 donors (24.6%) had hepatic arterial

variants (Type II to Type XII). The segment IV artery origi-
nated from the LHA, RHA, and PHA in 68 (45.0%), 44
(29.1%), and 38 potential donors (25.2%), respectively. Only
a single donor (0.7%) was found to have segment IV artery
which took off from the right gastric artery. Eight donors
(5.3%) had celiac trunk stenosis. Based on these ﬁndings,
there was no deﬁnite contraindication to LDLT in terms of
hepatic arterial variants.
Conventional portal vein anatomy with a bifurcating main
portal vein (MPV) was observed in 129 potential donors
(85.4%), while signiﬁcant variation in the portal venous sys-
tem was found in 22 donors (14.6%). Variations included
trifurcation in 14 cases, right anterior portal vein (RAPV)
take-off from the left portal vein (LPV) in four cases (Fig. 2a),
LPV from the RAPV in one case (Fig. 2b), and right posterior
portal vein (RPPV) originating from the MPV in three cases.
The most common hepatic venous variation was the
presence of right inferior hepatic vein in 93 potential
donors, followed by LHV and MHV forming a common trunk
in 17 donors, and venous drainage from segment I into the
IVC in three donors. In contrast, conventional hepatic
venous drainage was recognized in 46 potential donors
(30.5%).
Living donor liver transplantation selection
A total of 47 out of the potential 151 donors surveyed
eventually underwent graft harvest, of whom 43 donated
the right hepatic lobe and four donated the left lobe. The
oldest donor was about 56 years old. The surgical success

Among the 22 potential donors with signiﬁcant portal
variants, six received liver graft harvest, while 16 were
excluded by our surgical team due to the complexity of
their portal vein variation. The remaining 88 potential do-
nors were excluded from graft harvest due to one or more
of the following reasons: <30% remnant volume (30.7%),
relatively small liver size for recipient (17.0%), moderate to
severe parenchyma steatosis (10.2%), recipient expired
(8.0%), living donor withdrew (8.0%), multiple immediate
siblings were available as donors for the same recipient
(6.8%), recipient was physically unﬁt for transplant (6.8%),
referral to another center (5.7%), living donor was medi-
cally unstable (5.7%), and anaphylactic shock during oper-
ation (1.1%) (Fig. 3).
Discussion
Previous studies showed similar outcomes and survival rates
in patients undergoing LDLT versus DDLT for hepatocellular
carcinoma [18], other benign liver disease [19], as well as in
pediatric groups [20]. Since LDLT has been proven effective
in alleviating the scarcity of cadaveric donors and given
that the number of cases is increasing, detailed preopera-
tive evaluation is crucial for the safety of both donors and
recipients.
Hepatic steatosis in the donor liver is known to reduce
parenchymal function. A previous study reported that with
an increase of 1% in hepatic fat content, the functional
mass of the donor liver will decrease by about 1% [21].
Therefore, macrovesicular steatosis greater than 30% he-
patic volume is believed to be a contraindication for liver
donation, owing to its association with increased risk of
graft failure [12,22]. In our center, about 5e6% of potential
living donors proved unsuitable for donation as a result of
moderate to severe fatty liver.
Vascular variations in potential living donors for LDLT are
of great surgical importance, and failure to properly char-
acterize them may lead to undesirable outcomes [23].
While previous authors have found no obvious vascular
variant discrepancy between Western and Asian pop-
ulations [4,5,9], each case must still be evaluated carefully.
In our study, 24.5% of potential living donors exhibited
signiﬁcant hepatic arterial variants. Although these varia-
tions do not constitute absolute contraindications for LDLT,
the transplant surgeon should be made aware of two spe-
ciﬁc variant types which may require more vascular ligation
and anastomosis. The ﬁrst is the variant artery of Michel
classiﬁcation type II, for donors whose planned surgical
plane is the LH, and the second is the variant artery of
Michel classiﬁcation type III if RH liver transplant is to be
performed.
Accurate identiﬁcation of the hepatic artery origin of
segment IV is also important. Investigators have found that
if the artery to segment IV from the RHA crosses the sur-
gical plane in the RH or LH donor group, there was an
increased risk of accidental artery ligation with resultant
ischemia [24]. It is therefore essential to preserve arterial
inﬂow to segment IV, in order to prevent ischemic change of
both the remaining liver in the living donor and graft failure

in the recipient [25]. In our study, segment IV artery origi-
nating from the LHA [Is this what you mean?] was most
commonly observed (45.0%), followed by 29.1% originating
from the RHA, while the remaining 25.2% took off from the
PHA.
Although celiac trunk stenosis was once considered an
exclusion criteria in LDLT owing to elevated risk of
ischemia, a more recent study showed that an intact
gastroduodenal artery and pancreaticoduodenal artery ar-
cade can provide adequate collateral perfusion to the
remnant liver of living donors [26]. In our study, celiac trunk
stenosis was present in 5.3% of potential donors, but was
not considered a contraindication for LDLT in any of the
donors.
Anatomically
signiﬁcant
portal
vein
variants
often
require
more
complicated
surgical
procedures
during
transplantation, which may increase the risk of post-
operative portal vein thrombosis [27,28]. Sahani et al. re-
ported that portal vein trifurcation may be considered a
contraindication for LDLT of segment VeVIII [29]. Others
have found that while portal vein variations may not
directly impact donor complications or recipient survival
rate in right lobe graft procedures, more challenging
reconstruction techniques may become necessary [30]. A

small group of potential donors in our study were found to
have a right anterior portal vein arising from the left portal
vein (Fig. 2a), which was considered an absolute contrain-
dication in a recent study [31]. Additionally, since portal
vein variants are usually accompanied by variations in bile
duct anatomy, precise delineation of these variations prior
to operation is imperative. Although not considered to be
an absolute contraindication for liver grafting at our center,
16 potential donors were excluded by our transplant sur-
geons in this study. One of the reasons that these cases
were excluded was the fact that they were evaluated early
in the case series at a point on the learning curve where our
physicians were less experienced. In addition, the re-
cipients may have had other suitable donors. Success in
these cases will largely depend on the surgeon’s conﬁdence
in performing a potentially complicated transplant with
multiple vascular anastomosis, and any evaluations should
be conducted on a case-by-case basis by a multidisciplinary
team.
The most common hepatic venous variation in our study
was the existence of right inferior hepatic veins (61.6%),
which was a greater prevalence than that found in a pre-
vious study (47%) [27]. If a large right accessory inferior
hepatic vein (i.e., cross-sectional diameter �5 mm) [3] is
transected during surgery, hepatic sectors that depend on
it for drainage may develop congestion and delayed
ischemia, with resulting degradation in functional graft
volume. Consequently, this vessel should be preserved and
then reattached to the recipient’s IVC. The distance be-
tween the opening of a large right accessory inferior he-
patic vein and the hepatic venous conﬂuence should be
measured. If the distance is > 4 cm, there is higher risk of
increased surgical time and increased risk of graft mal-
function [32].
Automated MDCT-based liver volumetric measurement
allows accurate assessment of TV, DV, and RV, and is more
efﬁcient than manual methods [33,34]. Adequate RV and
DV must be matched to the metabolic demands of the
living donor and recipient, respectively, in order to mini-
mize the donor morbidity rate. More speciﬁcally, the RV of
a living donor should be at least 30% of TV to maintain
basic liver function [35]. Sufﬁcient DV must also be
considered to prevent small-for-size syndrome of hyper-
bilirubinemia, ascites, or graft failure. Generally, GRBWR
should be at least 0.8% as a minimal requirement for LDLT.
However, a recent study demonstrated that living donors
younger than 44 years of age with GRBWR <0.8% can also
undergo RH donation procedure safely [36]. In our study,
27 cases (25.7%) were excluded due to RV < 30%, and 15
cases (14.3%) were excluded due to a relatively small liver
size for the recipient, with a mean GRBWR of less than

0.7%. Therefore, insufﬁcient liver volume was the single
most common etiology for exclusion of potential living
donors at our center, a ﬁnding that is consistent with other
studies [5,9].
Detection of vascular variance and volumetric mea-
surement may be inﬂuenced by several factors. First,
contrast-to-noise ratio of the vessel to liver was related to
body size, heart function, the concentration of contrast
medium, and the scan time of living donors. Second, severe
fatty liver with low-attenuated parenchyma may confuse
the software and cause erroneous delineation of liver edge
during volumetric measurement. Routine veriﬁcation of the
liver boundary is suggested during measurement.
Currently, several imaging modalities are used for pre-
operative survey for LDLT. MDCT and MRI can both provide
more detail than ultrasound [37]. Although MRI is excellent
for steatosis evaluation, it requires a relatively complex
protocol, while MDCT can deliver fatty liver quantiﬁcation
with similar accuracy in detection of moderate to severe
hepatic steatosis and at lower cost [31]. Kodama Y. et al.
reported that unenhanced CT is considered the best
method for measuring the pathologic fatty content of the
liver [11]. For vascular variation assessment, MDCT is

preferable to MRI due to better spatial resolution and image
quality [38]. MRI also suffers from relatively lower contrast
and smaller edge magnitudes, which may inﬂuence the
accuracy of volumetric measurements [39]. While MDCT has
the disadvantage of ionizing radiation, MRI is relatively
expensive, time-consuming, and easily disturbed by motion
artifacts. In our center, MDCT is the primary imaging mo-
dality for preoperative survey due to the considerations
stated above. However, MDCT may be ineffective for
evaluating
the
biliary
system
without
hepatobiliary-
excreted contrast agent.
Although magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography
(MRCP) is considered the gold standard for preoperative
biliary evaluation, CT cholangiography and intraoperative
cholangiography can also accurately assess biliary anatomy
[40]. Bile duct variants are not considered absolute con-
traindications, and no transplantation was terminated in
our study as a result of intraoperative cholangiography.
In our center, MRCP is not routinely performed for biliary
system evaluation in LDLT. Intraoperative cholangiography
by the transplant surgeon is used as an alternative tool for
preoperative biliary evaluation. A potential limitation is
that MDCT may have relatively low sensitivity for the
detection of mild steatosis (less than 30% steatosis) as
compared to MRI, and additional MRI studies may be
required in the future for more precise fatty liver evalua-
tion in such situations. Moreover, this was a single-center
study with a limited number of LH cases, more data are
needed.
For surveys of potential living donors, MDCT can provide
imaging studies of liver parenchyma steatosis and vascular
variants with far greater detail, and allows more accurate
volumetric measurement compared with other modalities.
In this study, the most common exclusion etiology was
insufﬁcient RV and DV, followed by moderate to severe
fatty liver.
